## NN

In the following sections we evaluate whether NN and SVM models improve demand prediction. The target, features and preprocessing are shown in @tbl-nn-target-features. We compare the models with an always zero prediction and a spatial × time × weekday mean. The second baseline is stronger because it already represents the main recurring demand patterns. Our primary metric is MAE. It measures the average absolute difference between predicted and observed trips. The baseline results are shown in @tbl-trivial-baseline-test-mae.

The NN development consists of a baseline model, a two stage grid search and final retraining. The baseline model was trained for every spatial and temporal configuration. It uses two hidden layers with 64 and 32 nodes, ReLU activations and a spatial bias. Numerical inputs were standardized using training data only. The full architecture and training configuration are reported in @tbl-nn-baseline-architecture and @tbl-nn-baseline-training.
The best baseline checkpoint for each configuration was selected by validation MAE. Raw MAE values cannot be compared directly across aggregation levels because the demand scale changes. We therefore also use an MAE Skill Score relative to the spatial × time × weekday baseline. A positive value means that the NN improves on this baseline. Only Census Tracts at 1 hour resolution achieve a positive score. The improvement is very small at 0.0043. The 24 hour models perform worst. This may partly result from their smaller training sets. Diagnostics for Census Tracts at 1 hour also show that the model has particular difficulty with high demand. The complete baseline results and diagnostics are shown in @tbl-nn-baseline-results and @fig-nn-baseline-diagnostics. 
These findings led us to focus on positive demand during the grid search. We used Balanced MAE for model selection. It gives equal importance to zero and positive demand observations. Stage one compared standard training, positive demand weighting and undersampling. The tested configurations are reported in @tbl-nn-grid-stage-one. All stage one models remained below the spatial × time × weekday baseline. However, weighting performed consistently better than undersampling. Stage two therefore combined the most promising weighting strategies with different architectures and learning rates. The search space and results are shown in @tbl-nn-grid-stage-two and @tbl-nn-grid-performance.
Model S2-7 performed best in the grid search. It uses hidden layers with 128 and 64 nodes, a learning rate of 0.001 and a weight of 5 for positive demand. It reached a validation Balanced MAE of 2.7877 and an MAE Skill Score of 0.0014. The best result occurred in epoch 29 of 30. This supported retraining with a larger epoch budget. Its training history is shown in @fig-nn-grid-winner-history.
The final model uses this configuration with up to 100 epochs and an early stopping patience of 10. The checkpoint selected at epoch 26 achieved a validation Balanced MAE of 2.9319. On the TEST set, the model achieved a Balanced MAE of 2.8775 and an MAE Skill Score of 0.0253. This represents only a small improvement over the spatial × time × weekday baseline.
The difference between demand groups is very important for operations. The zero demand MAE is 0.0123, while the positive demand MAE is 5.7427. Peak demand MAE rises to 17.1399. Despite positive demand weighting, the model remains much more accurate when no trips occur. Precision is 0.8123 and recall is 0.7162. The model is therefore relatively reliable when it predicts demand, but it misses part of the observed demand. The full TEST results are shown in @tbl-final-census-tract-1h-test-scores and @fig-final-census-tract-test-mae.
The selected configuration was also trained on the other spatial and temporal datasets. However, its settings were tuned only on Census Tracts at 1 hour resolution. The comparison in @fig-final-mae-skill-trivial-baselines therefore shows how well the configuration transfers. It does not compare separately optimized models for every dataset. Improvements through lagged demand and a two stage prediction approach are discussed in the outlook.

## NN compared to SVM

We compare both models on the same TEST observations. The NN performs better on most error metrics and has higher precision. The SVM achieves higher recall across all configurations. It detects more demand intervals, but it also produces more false demand signals. The NN is more conservative, although the SVM performs better on several metrics for H3 resolution 7 at 24 hours. The number of metric wins is reported in @tbl-final-nn-svm-metric-wins.
The demand bucket comparison provides a more detailed view. For Census Tracts at 1 hour, the SVM has slightly lower MAE for intervals with 1 or 2 to 3 trips. The NN performs better from 4 trips onwards. Its advantage grows at high demand. These results are shown in @fig-final-census-tract-1h-demand-bucket-mae. The complete comparison across datasets is presented in @fig-final-nn-svm-pipeline-comparison.
Both models usually improve on the always zero prediction. This is a weak benchmark because it does not support useful fleet operations. The stronger spatial × time × weekday baseline is only outperformed by the NN for Census Tracts at 1 hour. With the current data and features, the additional complexity of both model pipelines creates little operational value.

```{python}
#| label: fig-final-mae-skill-trivial-baselines
#| fig-cap: "Test MAE skill scores of NN and SVM models against both baselines."
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| out-width: 80%
#| fig-align: center

from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.ticker import PercentFormatter
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

comparison_metrics_path = Path(
    "results/appendix/svm_nn_model_metrics.parquet"
)
if not comparison_metrics_path.exists():
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Missing NN-SVM comparison metrics: {comparison_metrics_path}. "
        "Run the NN-SVM comparison notebook before rendering the report."
    )

skill_metrics = pd.read_parquet(
    comparison_metrics_path,
    columns=[
        "dataset",
        "model",
        "mae_skill_vs_zero",
        "mae_skill_vs_spatial_time_weekday_mean",
    ],
)
dataset_order = [
    "census_tracts_1h",
    "census_tracts_4h",
    "census_tracts_24h",
    "community_areas_1h",
    "community_areas_4h",
    "community_areas_24h",
    "hexagon_h3r7_1h",
    "hexagon_h3r7_4h",
    "hexagon_h3r7_24h",
]
dataset_labels = {
    "census_tracts_1h": "Census tracts · 1H",
    "census_tracts_4h": "Census tracts · 4H",
    "census_tracts_24h": "Census tracts · 24H",
    "community_areas_1h": "Community areas · 1H",
    "community_areas_4h": "Community areas · 4H",
    "community_areas_24h": "Community areas · 24H",
    "hexagon_h3r7_1h": "H3 resolution 7 · 1H",
    "hexagon_h3r7_4h": "H3 resolution 7 · 4H",
    "hexagon_h3r7_24h": "H3 resolution 7 · 24H",
}
expected_pairs = pd.MultiIndex.from_product(
    [dataset_order, ["NN", "SVM"]],
    names=["dataset", "model"],
)
actual_pairs = pd.MultiIndex.from_frame(
    skill_metrics[["dataset", "model"]]
)
if (
    len(expected_pairs.difference(actual_pairs))
    or skill_metrics.duplicated(["dataset", "model"]).any()
):
    raise ValueError(
        "Expected exactly one NN and one SVM row for every dataset."
    )

plot_specs = [
    (
        "mae_skill_vs_zero",
        "MAE skill vs. zero-demand baseline",
    ),
    (
        "mae_skill_vs_spatial_time_weekday_mean",
        "MAE skill vs. spatial × time × weekday baseline",
    ),
]
model_colors = {
    "NN": "#1f77b4",
    "SVM": "#ff7f0e",
}
dataset_positions = np.arange(len(dataset_order))
bar_width = 0.38

figure, axes = plt.subplots(
    2,
    1,
    figsize=(13.5, 9.5),
    sharex=True,
    constrained_layout=True,
)
for axis, (metric, title) in zip(axes, plot_specs):
    for offset, model in (
        (-bar_width / 2, "NN"),
        (bar_width / 2, "SVM"),
    ):
        values = (
            skill_metrics.loc[
                lambda frame: frame["model"].eq(model),
                ["dataset", metric],
            ]
            .set_index("dataset")
            .reindex(dataset_order)[metric]
            .to_numpy()
        )
        axis.bar(
            dataset_positions + offset,
            values,
            bar_width,
            label=model,
            color=model_colors[model],
        )

    axis.axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=1)
    axis.set_title(title, loc="left")
    axis.set_ylabel("MAE skill score")
    axis.yaxis.set_major_formatter(PercentFormatter(xmax=1.0))
    axis.grid(axis="y", alpha=0.25)
    axis.legend(frameon=False, ncols=2)

axes[-1].set_xticks(dataset_positions)
axes[-1].set_xticklabels(
    [dataset_labels[dataset] for dataset in dataset_order],
    rotation=35,
    ha="right",
)
figure.suptitle(
    "MAE skill scores by model and dataset",
    fontsize=15,
)
plt.show()
```

For the pilot, we therefore recommend the spatial × time × weekday baseline. It is simple, transparent and inexpensive to maintain. The current NN and SVM pipelines should not be used as the only basis for fleet dispatch. This result does not show that NNs are generally better than SVMs. It only applies to the pipelines and data evaluated in this report. A follow up project with additional information and a model designed for different demand levels may provide more value.
